questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is the main difference between functional testing and performance testing?

options.A: Functional testing happens only after release, and performance testing happens only before release
options.B: Functional testing is always automated, and performance testing is always manual
options.C: Functional testing checks speed, and performance testing checks correctness of the output
options.D: Functional testing checks correctness; performance testing checks speed and behavior under load

questions.explanation: Functional tests verify correct behavior, while performance tests measure responsiveness, throughput and resource use under varying conditions. A feature can be functionally correct and still perform poorly.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What does "capacity" mean in the context of performance testing?

options.A: The number of test cases that have been automated so far
options.B: The physical size of the servers that host the application
options.C: The number of developers who are available to fix performance defects
options.D: The maximum workload a system can handle while still meeting its requirements

questions.explanation: Capacity describes the highest load level at which the system still meets its defined performance criteria, which is what capacity or scalability tests aim to find.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which of these is an example of a non-functional performance requirement?

options.A: The search page must display the company logo in the top-left corner
options.B: The search feature must return results that match the keywords entered by the user
options.C: 95% of search requests must complete within 2 seconds under 500 concurrent users
options.D: The search feature must be available in five different languages

questions.explanation: A performance requirement specifies a measurable target for speed, capacity or resource use under stated conditions. Correctness, layout and language support are functional or usability requirements.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is degradation testing intended to observe?

options.A: How easily a user interface can be translated into other languages
options.B: How quickly developers can add new features to a system
options.C: How well documentation describes the system's functional requirements
options.D: How gracefully a system behaves as it approaches or exceeds its capacity limits

questions.explanation: Degradation testing checks whether performance declines gradually and predictably, or fails abruptly, as load increases beyond normal levels.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which of the following is most likely to cause performance problems that stem from the software architecture?

options.A: Sequential, blocking calls to other services for one request
options.B: A user interface that uses a color scheme with low contrast
options.C: A help page written in language that is hard for beginners to understand
options.D: A login form that requires a password of at least eight characters

questions.explanation: Chatty, sequential architectures multiply latency because each call waits for the previous one, which is a structural cause of poor performance rather than a coding or configuration slip.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Why might a system pass all functional tests but still be unacceptable to users in production?

options.A: Production traffic is always lower than the traffic used in functional testing
options.B: Functional tests always include performance checks, so this situation cannot occur
options.C: Users always prefer software that fails functional tests over software that is slow
options.D: It may be too slow or unable to handle real user volumes even though its outputs are correct

questions.explanation: Functional correctness says nothing about speed or capacity. A correct feature that is too slow, or that collapses under real traffic, still disappoints users.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is meant by a system's "operational profile" in performance testing?

options.A: A record of every bug that has been reported against the system
options.B: It may be too slow or unable to handle real volumes despite correct output
options.C: A list of the job titles of the people who operate the servers
options.D: The physical location where the servers of the system are installed

questions.explanation: An operational profile captures realistic usage patterns, such as which functions are used and how often, which is used to build a representative test workload.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which best describes the goal of capacity testing, as distinct from load testing at a single fixed level?

options.A: Determining whether all functional requirements have been implemented
options.B: Determining how many lines of code the application contains
options.C: Determining the maximum workload the system can sustain while still meeting requirements
options.D: Determining whether the user interface looks correct on a mobile phone screen

questions.explanation: Capacity testing seeks the upper limit of acceptable performance, often by increasing load until requirements are no longer met, rather than testing at one predetermined level.

questions.question: Which additional information does the 95th percentile response time give beyond the average?

options.A: It shows the number of requests that failed during the test
options.B: Determining the maximum workload the system can sustain and still meet requirements
options.C: It shows the exact response time that every single request received
options.D: It shows the total memory used by the application server during the test

questions.explanation: A percentile describes the distribution's tail, so the 95th percentile shows how bad the slower requests are, which the average alone can hide.

questions.question: What does "throughput" measure in a performance test?

options.A: The percentage of CPU that is idle during the test
options.B: It shows the response time experienced by the slowest 5% of requests
options.C: The number of test cases that were automated for the release
options.D: The number of virtual users configured in the test script

questions.explanation: Throughput is a rate, commonly expressed as transactions or requests per second, that shows how much work the system is completing.

questions.question: What does high CPU "utilization" on a server indicate?

options.A: The server is running an outdated operating system
options.B: The CPU has a very large amount of installed memory
options.C: The server has many network cables connected to it
options.D: The number of transactions processed by the system per unit of time

questions.explanation: Utilization is the fraction of a resource's capacity that is in use over a period, so high CPU utilization means the processor is busy most of the time.

questions.question: Why is response time alone not always sufficient to judge whether a system is ready for production?

options.A: Response time always improves as more users are added to the system
options.B: Response time can never be measured accurately by any tool
options.C: Response time is only relevant for systems without a user interface
options.D: It ignores throughput, error rate and resource usage that also matter

questions.explanation: A full performance picture combines response time with throughput, errors and resource consumption, since a fast response under one condition may hide problems under another.

questions.question: Which measure describes the number of users interacting with a system at the same time?

options.A: Concurrent users
options.B: Idle users
options.C: Registered users
options.D: Licensed users

questions.explanation: Concurrent users refers to those actively using the system simultaneously, which drives load, unlike the total number of accounts that exist.

questions.question: What is a "bottleneck" in the context of performance testing?

options.A: A resource or component that limits overall throughput or response time
options.B: A type of test environment used only for security testing
options.C: A document that records the functional requirements of the system
options.D: A tool used to generate synthetic load against the system

questions.explanation: A bottleneck is the constraining resource, such as CPU, database or network, whose limits determine how far the system can scale before performance suffers.

questions.question: Which of the following is a resource-utilization metric commonly monitored during a performance test?

options.A: Memory usage on the application server
options.B: The number of open browser tabs on the tester's laptop
options.C: The number of commits made to the source code repository that day
options.D: The number of words in the requirements document

questions.explanation: Resource metrics such as CPU, memory, disk and network usage on the systems under test show where capacity is being consumed and where a bottleneck may exist.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: What is the main benefit of considering performance requirements during the requirements phase?

options.A: Performance expectations are clear early, guiding design before it's costly to change
options.B: It allows performance testing to be skipped entirely during development
options.C: It guarantees that the final system will have no performance defects
options.D: It removes the need to run any performance tests later in the project

questions.explanation: Setting expectations early lets architecture and design account for them, since fixing structural performance problems late in a project is far more expensive.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why is it useful to performance test individual components early, before full system integration?

options.A: Component-level testing removes the need to test the integrated system later
options.B: Component-level testing always finds every performance problem that could ever occur
options.C: Component-level issues can be found and fixed while they are still cheap and isolated to address
options.D: Component-level testing can only be done after the software has been released

questions.explanation: Testing early at a smaller scope catches structural or coding issues before they are compounded by integration, when they become harder and more costly to diagnose.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why should performance testing not be left until immediately before a planned release?

options.A: Performance defects can only be found in the days before a release
options.B: Performance test results are always more accurate close to a release date
options.C: Development teams work faster in the final week before a release
options.D: There is little time to fix any issues found and to retest after the fixes are applied

questions.explanation: Testing late leaves no slack for redesign or retesting if a problem is found, which increases the risk of shipping with unresolved performance issues or delaying the release.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: What is a reasonable performance-related addition to a team's Definition of Done for a user story?

options.A: The story has been translated into every language supported by the product
options.B: The story has been reviewed by at least ten different people
options.C: The story's key operations meet an agreed response-time target under a representative load
options.D: The story includes a screenshot of the user interface on every possible device

questions.explanation: Adding an explicit, testable performance criterion keeps performance visible throughout development rather than treating it as an afterthought.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why might early performance testing use simplified or scaled-down prototypes rather than the full system?

options.A: Prototypes always give more accurate results than a fully built system
options.B: Objectives, scope, workload, environment, schedule and acceptance criteria
options.C: Prototypes are required by law before any software can be released
options.D: Prototypes remove the need for any further testing once the system is complete

questions.explanation: Early in a project, a full implementation may not be available, so testing a scaled-down version gives an early indication of risk before waiting for the complete build.

questions.question: Which activity typically comes first in a performance testing project?

options.A: Executing the full-scale performance test against production
options.B: Identifying performance risks and defining objectives and requirements
options.C: Writing the final summary report for management
options.D: Archiving the test scripts after the project has ended

questions.explanation: Planning starts with understanding risks and defining what "acceptable" performance means, before any test design or execution can meaningfully begin.

questions.question: Which activity involves creating the scripts and test data needed to simulate realistic user behavior?

options.A: Post-project retrospective
options.B: Test design and implementation
options.C: Results reporting to stakeholders
options.D: Test planning and risk analysis

questions.explanation: Design and implementation is where scripts, data and workload models are built to reproduce the behavior identified during planning and analysis.

questions.question: During test execution, which practice helps ensure results can be trusted?

options.A: Allowing other unrelated work to run on the same servers during the test
options.B: Running the test only once, since repeating it wastes time
options.C: Stopping all monitoring so that the system is not slowed down by observation
options.D: Capturing dynamic values from a response and reusing them in later requests

questions.explanation: Watching for problems with the environment or the load itself during execution helps catch invalid runs early, rather than analyzing flawed data afterward.

questions.question: What does analyzing performance test results mainly involve?

options.A: Counting how many virtual users were configured in the test tool
options.B: Deleting any results that do not match the expected outcome
options.C: Gradually increasing virtual users over time instead of starting all at once
options.D: Rewriting the functional requirements to match whatever was measured

questions.explanation: Analysis compares outcomes to targets and digs into metrics to understand why a target was or was not met, which is more than simply recording pass or fail.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a baseline performance test?

options.A: To replace the need for any further performance testing on the project
options.B: To find every functional defect in the system before release
options.C: To establish a reference point that later test results can be compared against
options.D: To measure how many developers worked on the current release

questions.explanation: A baseline gives a known reference under stable conditions, which makes later comparisons, such as checking whether a change caused a regression, meaningful.

questions.question: What is a common output of the test design activity in a performance testing project?

options.A: A finalized budget for the entire performance testing program
options.B: A list of every employee in the organization's IT department
options.C: A signed contract with the vendor of the testing tool
options.D: A set of workload models and scripted transactions ready to be executed

questions.explanation: Design turns the objectives and risks identified earlier into concrete, executable workload models and scripts that can be run in the next activity.

questions.question: What is the basic structure of a typical performance test script?

options.A: Only comments describing what the test intends to do
options.B: Producing simulated traffic against the system, standing in for real users
options.C: A single line of code that starts the whole test in one step
options.D: A list of every developer who has worked on the application

questions.explanation: Scripts generally start with setup, contain the transactions that represent what a user does, and end with clean-up, which mirrors a realistic user session.

questions.question: Why is parameterizing test data important in a load test with many virtual users?

options.A: To capture the effect of network latency for users in different regions
options.B: It makes the test script shorter and therefore easier to read
options.C: It removes the need to define any workload model for the test
options.D: It guarantees that the test will find every performance defect

questions.explanation: Without varied data, all requests might hit the same cache entry or database row, producing results that do not reflect how real, varied users behave.

questions.question: What does "correlation" mean in the context of performance test scripting?

options.A: Calculating the correlation coefficient between CPU and memory usage
options.B: Comparing the results of two separate performance test projects
options.C: Choosing which programming language the test tool is written in
options.D: Collecting metrics such as CPU, memory and response time while the test runs

questions.explanation: Many applications return session-specific values, such as tokens, that must be captured and replayed correctly, or the recorded script will fail against the live system.

questions.question: What does "ramp-up" refer to in a load test?

options.A: Raising the physical temperature of the server room during a test
options.B: Adding new functional requirements partway through the test
options.C: Increasing the price of the license for the testing tool
options.D: Compatibility with the protocols and technologies used by the SUT

questions.explanation: A gradual ramp-up avoids an artificial, all-at-once surge and lets the system and monitoring reach a steady state in a controlled way.

questions.question: What is the purpose of "think time" in a load test script?

options.A: Providing detailed, code-level visibility into transactions as they execute
options.B: Giving the load-testing tool time to compile the script before running it
options.C: Reducing the number of virtual users needed to reach a target throughput
options.D: Extending the total duration of the test without adding any load

questions.explanation: Real users pause to read or think, and omitting this pause creates an unrealistically aggressive workload that does not represent actual usage.

questions.question: Why do many performance testing tools support recording user actions in a browser or client, rather than requiring scripts to be written entirely by hand?

options.A: Commercial tools often add vendor support and polished reporting
options.B: Recording is only possible for applications that have no user interface at all
options.C: Recording removes the need to ever run the resulting script against the system under test
options.D: Recording guarantees the script will work correctly without any further changes

questions.explanation: Recording speeds up initial script creation by capturing actual requests, though the raw recording usually still needs correlation and parameterization before it is realistic.

questions.question: Why would a team run load generators from multiple, geographically distributed locations?

options.A: To avoid having to write any test scripts at all
options.B: To make the test easier to run from a single laptop
options.C: To reduce the total cost of the testing tool license
options.D: Recording captures real interactions quickly as a starting point to refine

questions.explanation: Users spread across regions experience different network conditions, and distributed generators reproduce that variation instead of measuring only local latency.

questions.question: What is the role of a monitoring tool during a performance test?

options.A: Managing which developers have access to the source code repository
options.B: Writing the functional test cases used earlier in the project
options.C: The expected real-world concurrent usage the system needs to support
options.D: Generating the simulated load that is sent to the system under test

questions.explanation: Monitoring tools observe the system's internal state during a test, which is essential for finding the cause of any performance problem the load reveals.

questions.question: What is a key difference between an open-source and a commercial performance testing tool that a team should weigh during selection?

options.A: More simulated concurrent load typically needs more licensed capacity
options.B: Open-source tools cannot be used by any organization for commercial projects
options.C: Open-source tools can never generate any load against a real system
options.D: Commercial tools are always faster at generating load than any open-source tool

questions.explanation: The trade-off is typically support, integration and reporting convenience versus licensing cost and reliance on internal skills, not a fundamental difference in load-generation capability.

questions.question: What is Application Performance Monitoring (APM) tooling commonly used for?

options.A: Managing the budget allocated to the performance testing project
options.B: Designing the visual layout of a web application's pages
options.C: Writing the marketing copy that describes a new product release
options.D: Scalability testing

questions.explanation: APM tools trace transactions inside the application, often down to the method or database call level, which helps pinpoint where time is spent internally.

questions.question: What is a risk of relying on a single all-in-one monitoring tool without any independent verification?

options.A: It will always report exactly the same numbers as every other tool on the market
options.B: It automatically fixes any performance defects that it detects
options.C: Its own instrumentation overhead or blind spots could distort or miss important results
options.D: It removes the need to record test results in any report at all

questions.explanation: Every monitoring tool has some overhead and coverage limits, so relying on one without cross-checking risks missing or misrepresenting the true picture.

questions.question: Why might a performance testing tool license be priced by the number of virtual users it can simulate?

options.A: Generating more simulated concurrent load typically requires more licensed capacity from the vendor
options.B: The number of virtual users has no relationship to how a testing tool is typically licensed
options.C: Every performance testing tool on the market is provided completely free of charge
options.D: Licensing by virtual users is done only to make the tool's pricing page look more complex

questions.explanation: Many commercial tools scale their license cost with the amount of simulated load they can generate, since that capacity is central to what the tool provides.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which term describes testing a system's behavior as the number of users or data volume grows over time?

options.A: Usability testing
options.B: Scalability testing
options.C: Accessibility testing
options.D: Compatibility testing

questions.explanation: Scalability testing checks whether performance stays acceptable as load or data size increases, which is distinct from usability, compatibility or accessibility concerns.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which testing type keeps a system under a sustained, realistic load for an extended period, such as many hours or days?

options.A: Smoke testing
options.B: Regression testing
options.C: Endurance (soak) testing
options.D: Unit testing

questions.explanation: Endurance testing runs a steady load for a long duration to reveal issues such as memory leaks that only appear over time, unlike short functional test types.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which testing type applies a sudden, sharp increase in load to see how the system copes?

options.A: Boundary value testing
options.B: Exploratory testing
options.C: Static testing
options.D: Spike testing

questions.explanation: Spike testing simulates a sudden burst, such as a flash sale, to see whether the system handles the abrupt change gracefully.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which testing type deliberately pushes a system beyond its expected operating limits to find its breaking point?

options.A: Installation testing
options.B: Smoke testing
options.C: Confirmation testing
options.D: Stress testing

questions.explanation: Stress testing goes past normal expected conditions to see how and where the system fails, and whether it fails gracefully.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of load testing?

options.A: Evaluating system behavior under an expected, realistic level of concurrent usage
options.B: Checking that the application looks correct on different screen sizes
options.C: Ensuring the source code follows the team's coding style guide
options.D: Verifying that individual functions return the correct output

questions.explanation: Load testing exercises the system at expected or peak realistic usage levels to confirm it performs acceptably, rather than checking correctness or style.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What does "reliability" mean in the context of performance under load?

options.A: The system has been reviewed and approved by the security team
options.B: Stress testing
options.C: The system's user interface uses consistent fonts and colors throughout
options.D: The system's source code has been documented in detail

questions.explanation: Reliability under load concerns whether the system keeps working correctly and consistently as load is applied, not its visual or documentation qualities.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Why is it problematic for a performance requirement to state only "the system must be fast"?

options.A: It is too specific to be understood by anyone reading the requirement
options.B: It cannot be objectively measured or verified without a specific target and condition
options.C: It guarantees that testers will agree on exactly what to measure
options.D: It automatically becomes a functional requirement instead of a performance one

questions.explanation: A testable requirement needs a measurable target, such as a response time under stated conditions; a vague adjective like "fast" cannot be verified or agreed upon.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Why is availability often considered alongside performance in non-functional requirements?

options.A: Availability has no relationship to performance testing at all
options.B: Availability is only relevant to systems that have no users
options.C: Availability and performance are always measured with exactly the same tool
options.D: An unavailable system has effectively infinite response time from a user's perspective

questions.explanation: A system that is down provides no response at all, which is the most extreme case of poor performance, so the two concerns are closely linked.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates a performance problem caused by database design rather than application code?

options.A: An error message is displayed in the wrong language for the user
options.B: Evaluating system behavior under an expected, realistic concurrent usage
options.C: A report is generated in a file format the user did not request
options.D: A button on a form is labeled with a misspelled word

questions.explanation: Missing indexes are a classic database-level cause of degrading query performance as data volume increases, unrelated to labels, language or file format issues.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is the relationship between performance testing and capacity planning?

options.A: Capacity planning is only performed by the marketing department
options.B: Performance test results provide data that capacity planning uses to forecast future infrastructure needs
options.C: Capacity planning replaces the need for any performance testing
options.D: Performance testing and capacity planning are unrelated activities in every organization

questions.explanation: Measured throughput and resource usage under known loads give capacity planners the evidence needed to project how infrastructure needs will grow.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which of these best describes "elasticity" in a cloud-hosted system?

options.A: The number of programming languages that a development team can use
options.B: The physical flexibility of the cables connecting servers in a data center
options.C: The ability of a user interface to resize itself for different screen widths
options.D: The ability to automatically add or remove resources in response to changing load

questions.explanation: Elasticity refers to a system's or platform's capability to scale resources up or down automatically as demand changes, which performance testing can help validate.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Why can a system that performs well in a test environment still perform poorly in production?

options.A: Performance testing tools always overestimate real production capacity
options.B: Production systems can never experience more load than a test environment
options.C: Production may have different data volumes, configurations, network conditions or real user behavior
options.D: Production environments are always identical to every test environment by definition

questions.explanation: Differences between environments, such as scale, configuration and traffic patterns, mean a clean test result does not automatically guarantee the same outcome in production.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is the purpose of defining a "workload model" before running a performance test?

options.A: To describe the reporting hierarchy of the performance testing team
options.B: A description of how the system is actually used, including operation mix
options.C: To describe how the source code of the application is structured internally
options.D: To describe the color palette used throughout the user interface

questions.explanation: A workload model translates real or expected usage patterns into a testable specification, so the applied load reflects reality rather than an arbitrary guess.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: Which of the following would most directly help reduce the risk of an architecture-driven performance problem going unnoticed until late in a project?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on user interface styling throughout the project
options.B: Waiting until the user acceptance testing phase to think about performance for the first time
options.C: Delaying all performance-related discussions until after the system is in production
options.D: Reviewing the architecture for potential bottlenecks and testing key components early

questions.explanation: Structural issues are cheapest to catch and fix early, through architectural review and early component testing, rather than being discovered for the first time near release or after launch.

questions.question: Which pair of metrics, considered together, gives a fuller picture of system performance than either alone?

options.A: Response time and throughput
options.B: Font size and background color
options.C: Number of developers and number of meetings held
options.D: Number of test cases and number of testers

questions.explanation: Response time shows individual experience while throughput shows overall capacity; together they reveal trade-offs that neither metric alone would show.

questions.question: What does a rising error rate during a load test typically suggest?

options.A: The system is beginning to fail to handle requests correctly as load increases
options.B: The virtual users are behaving exactly like real production users
options.C: The test is almost finished and about to complete successfully
options.D: The monitoring tool has stopped collecting any further data

questions.explanation: An increasing rate of failed requests is a direct signal that the system is struggling under the applied load, which is central to interpreting test results.

questions.question: Why might two consecutive performance test runs under identical configured conditions produce slightly different results?

options.A: Performance testing tools always produce completely identical results on every single run
options.B: Test results are randomly generated and bear no relation to system behavior
options.C: Missing indexes are a classic database cause of degrading query performance
options.D: Any variation between runs always indicates a serious defect in the system

questions.explanation: Some variability is normal because real systems are not perfectly deterministic. Understanding this helps testers judge whether a difference is meaningful or just noise.

questions.question: What is a "service-level objective" in the context of performance testing?

options.A: A legal contract signed between two competing companies
options.B: A specific, measurable performance target that the system is expected to meet
options.C: A list of features that a product manager wants to build next
options.D: A description of the office hours during which support staff are available

questions.explanation: A service-level objective states a concrete goal, such as a response time or availability target, against which actual performance can be measured and judged.

questions.question: What does it mean when throughput stays flat even as the number of virtual users continues to increase?

options.A: The system is performing better as more users are added
options.B: The monitoring tool has a defect and cannot be trusted
options.C: The test has been configured with too many virtual users to be valid
options.D: Elasticity

questions.explanation: A throughput plateau despite growing load usually indicates a constraining resource has been reached, which is a classic bottleneck signal.

questions.question: Why do performance testers often prefer percentiles, such as the 95th or 99th, over the simple average when reporting response times?

options.A: Percentiles are easier to calculate than an average using any tool
options.B: Production may differ in data, configuration, network or real behavior
options.C: Percentiles remove the need to report throughput or error rate at all
options.D: Percentiles are always mathematically identical to the average in every data set

questions.explanation: An average can hide a long tail of slow requests; percentiles expose that tail directly, which matters because those slow requests are the ones users actually notice.

questions.question: What does a "check" typically refer to in the context of performance metrics?

options.A: To describe realistically how users and actions are distributed
options.B: A payment made to the vendor of the performance testing tool
options.C: A meeting held once a week to discuss unrelated topics
options.D: A document listing every developer working on the project

questions.explanation: In performance testing tools, a check evaluates a captured metric against a defined threshold, producing a pass or fail signal used in reporting.

questions.question: Which metric would most directly indicate that a connection pool to a database is saturated?

options.A: The number of test cases planned for the next release
options.B: The number of lines of code in the database access layer
options.C: The color scheme configured in the database administration tool
options.D: Reviewing the architecture and testing key components early

questions.explanation: When a limited pool of connections is fully used, new requests must wait, which shows up as growing wait time and response time rather than as a code-size or interface metric.

questions.question: What is the benefit of tracking both server-side and client-side timing during a performance test?

options.A: It removes the need to monitor CPU or memory usage on any server
options.B: It distinguishes delays caused by the back end from delays introduced by the network or the client
options.C: It doubles the total cost of running the performance test for no additional benefit
options.D: It guarantees that no performance defects will be found during the test

questions.explanation: Separating server and client timing helps pinpoint whether a slow user experience originates in the back end, the network, or client-side processing such as rendering.

questions.question: What is a reasonable interpretation of a load test in which the system passes all defined thresholds but resource utilization is already at 90% at the tested load?

options.A: The 90% utilization figure is not a meaningful metric to record in a report
options.B: The system meets today's requirement but may have little headroom for future growth
options.C: The result should be ignored, since passing a threshold means nothing at high utilization
options.D: The system has unlimited capacity and needs no further testing of any kind

questions.explanation: Passing a threshold with resources nearly exhausted signals limited headroom, which is a useful risk finding even though the test technically passed.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why do teams commonly reserve full-scale load tests for a scheduled cadence rather than running them on every single commit?

options.A: Full-scale load tests cannot produce any useful information about the system
options.B: Scheduling full-scale tests removes the need for any lightweight checks per build
options.C: It shows how well the system copes with a sudden, sharp load increase
options.D: Running a full-scale test more than once a year is against best practice

questions.explanation: Deep, resource-intensive tests do not fit the pace of frequent commits, so teams pair lightweight per-build checks with periodic full-scale runs to balance speed and depth.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why might a team include performance acceptance criteria as part of a release gate?

options.A: To reduce the number of features that are included in each release
options.B: To guarantee that the release will contain zero functional defects
options.C: To prevent a build that fails to meet agreed performance targets from being released
options.D: To remove the need for any monitoring once the system is in production

questions.explanation: A performance gate stops releases that do not meet agreed thresholds from progressing, which is a concrete way to make performance a release blocker rather than an afterthought.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why is a gradual, phased rollout to production sometimes preferred over releasing a change to all users at once?

options.A: Rising error rate suggests the system is failing to handle requests
options.B: It guarantees the release will contain no functional defects of any kind
options.C: It always takes less total time than releasing to everyone simultaneously
options.D: It removes the need to have monitored any pre-release performance test

questions.explanation: Limiting initial exposure caps the impact of a problem that only surfaces under genuine production load, giving a safety margin before wider exposure.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why is testing against a scaled-down environment, rather than a production-like one, a risk for performance conclusions?

options.A: Scaled-down environments remove the need to run any performance test at all
options.B: Production and scaled-down environments always behave identically in every case
options.C: Results may not extrapolate reliably to the different capacity and configuration of production
options.D: Scaled-down environments always produce more accurate results than production-like ones

questions.explanation: Differences in scale, hardware and configuration mean behavior observed on a small environment may not hold on production infrastructure, which limits how confidently results can be generalized.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: What activity should typically precede detailed test design in a performance testing project?

options.A: Archiving the scripts used in a previous, unrelated project
options.B: Identifying performance risks, objectives and requirements
options.C: Writing the final report that will be sent to executives
options.D: Purchasing office furniture for the testing team

questions.explanation: Design decisions depend on knowing what risks and requirements matter, so risk identification and objective-setting logically come first.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why is it valuable to involve operations staff early when planning performance testing?

options.A: Operations staff are legally required to approve every test script before it can run
options.B: Involving operations removes the need for any monitoring tools
options.C: They understand the production environment and can help ensure realistic test conditions
options.D: Operations staff always write all of the performance test scripts themselves

questions.explanation: Operations staff bring knowledge of real infrastructure, configuration and constraints, which helps the test environment and workload reflect reality.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: What does it mean to "shift left" performance testing?

options.A: Reducing the number of servers used in the test environment
options.B: Moving all performance testing to occur only after production release
options.C: Moving performance-related activities earlier in the development lifecycle
options.D: Rewriting all functional requirements using a different notation

questions.explanation: Shifting left means addressing performance earlier, such as during design and early development, rather than treating it as a final pre-release activity.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why might a team review performance results during a sprint retrospective?

options.A: To decide which programming language the team will use next
options.B: To assign blame to a specific individual for any performance issue found
options.C: To remove performance testing from the team's process going forward
options.D: To learn from what was measured and improve practices in future sprints

questions.explanation: Retrospectives support continuous improvement, and reviewing performance outcomes helps the team adjust practices, tooling or focus for subsequent work.

questions.question: Which activity in a performance testing project is most concerned with confirming that a test accurately represents intended conditions before results are trusted?

options.A: Monitoring the test environment and load during execution
options.B: Choosing office snacks for the testing team
options.C: Deciding on the final color scheme of the summary report
options.D: Selecting which conference the team will attend next year

questions.explanation: Confirming the environment and load behaved as intended during execution is what makes the resulting data trustworthy for later analysis.

questions.question: Why is it useful to run a performance test multiple times before drawing firm conclusions?

options.A: Repeating a test guarantees that the system will show improved performance each time
options.B: A single run may not represent typical behavior, and repetition shows whether results are consistent
options.C: Repeating a test removes the need to analyze the results afterward
options.D: Running a test only once always gives the most statistically reliable result

questions.explanation: Natural variability means a single run could be unusually good or bad; repeating the test helps distinguish a real pattern from a one-off fluctuation.

questions.question: What should happen when a performance test produces suspiciously good results compared to expectations?

options.A: Assume the system has been permanently and completely optimized
options.B: Delete the test script since it is clearly no longer needed
options.C: A specific, measurable performance target the system is expected to meet
options.D: Immediately publish the results as final without any further checking

questions.explanation: Unexpectedly good results can indicate a misconfigured test, such as cached data or an unrepresentative workload, so verifying validity before celebrating is good practice.

questions.question: Why should the configuration of the test environment be recorded alongside the results of a performance test?

options.A: It guarantees that future tests will not need any environment at all
options.B: It removes the need to record the actual performance metrics themselves
options.C: It allows the results to be correctly interpreted and reproduced later
options.D: It is a legal requirement in every country for any software project

questions.explanation: Without knowing the exact configuration used, later comparisons or reproductions of the test become unreliable, since even small setup differences can change results.

questions.question: What should a tester do if the load-testing tool itself reports an internal error partway through a scheduled test run?

options.A: Immediately conclude that the system under test has failed and stop all testing
options.B: Note the error, assess whether it invalidates the run, and decide whether to stop or restart it
options.C: Ignore the error completely and publish the partial results as if nothing happened
options.D: Delete the load-testing tool and switch to purely manual testing from then on

questions.explanation: A tool-side error can invalidate a run, so the tester should judge its impact and decide whether to restart or discard the affected data rather than treating it as a finding about the system.

questions.question: Why is it useful to compare results across multiple builds of the same feature over time, rather than looking at just one test?

options.A: It reveals performance trends and regressions that a single isolated test cannot show
options.B: A single test result is always more informative than any trend across several builds
options.C: Comparing across builds is never possible unless the builds are identical in every way
options.D: Comparing builds removes the need to define any acceptance criteria at all

questions.explanation: Trends across builds reveal whether performance is improving, stable or regressing over time, insight that one isolated measurement cannot provide by itself.

questions.question: Why might a performance test report distinguish between an "environment issue" and a genuine "product defect" when explaining a failed metric?

options.A: Making the distinction is only relevant for functional test reports, not performance ones
options.B: Environment issues are always more serious than any genuine product defect
options.C: Percentiles reveal how the slower requests performed, which averages hide
options.D: The distinction has no bearing on how the report should be written or acted upon

questions.explanation: Correctly attributing a failure's cause avoids wasted effort, since fixing a healthy product will not resolve a problem that actually originates in the environment.

questions.question: Why might a performance testing activity include a short "dry run" of the test script before the main scheduled execution?

options.A: A single measurement compared against a threshold, giving pass or fail
options.B: A dry run removes the need to monitor the system during the actual full test
options.C: A dry run is required by law before any performance test may be executed
options.D: A dry run guarantees that the full-scale test will pass every defined threshold

questions.explanation: A small trial run surfaces basic issues, such as a broken script step, cheaply and early, before investing the time and resources needed for the full-scale execution.

questions.question: What is a reasonable first diagnostic step when a load test shows response time rising sharply while throughput stays flat?

options.A: Check resource utilization on the servers and infrastructure to look for a saturated component
options.B: Reduce the number of virtual users to zero and stop investigating
options.C: Immediately rewrite the entire application from scratch without further investigation
options.D: Assume the monitoring tool is broken and ignore the result entirely

questions.explanation: That pattern often points to a bottleneck, so checking CPU, memory, database and network usage is a natural first step toward finding the constrained resource.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a ramp-down phase at the end of a load test?

options.A: It distinguishes back-end delays from network or client-side delays
options.B: Increasing the number of virtual users sharply right before the test ends
options.C: Doubling the license cost of the testing tool used
options.D: Deleting the test script immediately once the last user finishes

questions.explanation: A controlled ramp-down mirrors the ramp-up and avoids introducing an artificial event at the end of the test that could confuse the results.

questions.question: Why should a test script avoid hard-coding a specific record identifier, such as a single product ID, for all virtual users?

options.A: The system meets today's target but may have little headroom for growth
options.B: Hard-coded identifiers always make a test run faster than parameterized ones
options.C: Hard-coding removes the need to have any test data available at all
options.D: Hard-coding automatically improves the realism of a performance test

questions.explanation: A single shared identifier risks becoming unavailable mid-test and does not represent the variety of records that real users would actually access.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a lightweight performance smoke test in a pipeline?

options.A: Testing the smoke-detection hardware installed in the data center
options.B: Lightweight checks run per build, with deeper tests run less often
options.C: Replacing the need for any full-scale performance test ever
options.D: Verifying the visual design of the application's smoke-themed graphics

questions.explanation: A fast, minimal check catches gross regressions early and cheaply, saving full-scale testing for when it is warranted or scheduled.

questions.question: Why should performance test scripts be kept under version control, similar to application code?

options.A: Changes can be tracked, and previous versions of scripts can be recovered if needed
options.B: Version control guarantees that scripts will never need to be updated again
options.C: Version control automatically fixes any performance defects found by the scripts
options.D: Version control removes the need to document the test environment

questions.explanation: Scripts evolve alongside the application, and version control gives traceability and recoverability, just as it does for production source code.

questions.question: What should be verified before trusting results produced by a newly created test script?

options.A: It exposes a new version to a slice of traffic before a full rollout
options.B: That the script contains the largest possible number of virtual users
options.C: That the script was written by the most senior member of the team
options.D: That the script uses the most recently released version of the testing tool

questions.explanation: A new script's correctness should be confirmed, for example by validating request and response content, before its performance numbers are trusted for decision-making.

questions.question: Why is recording and replaying real production traffic sometimes used to build a performance test workload?

options.A: It removes the need to define an operational profile at all
options.B: It can produce a workload that closely reflects actual user behavior and patterns
options.C: It guarantees the test will use fewer virtual users than any other method
options.D: It is required by law in every jurisdiction before releasing software

questions.explanation: Replaying captured real traffic can be a practical way to approximate genuine usage patterns, complementing or substituting for a manually constructed workload model.

questions.question: Why might a load test unintentionally hammer a single backend resource if scripting is done carelessly?

options.A: Careless scripting removes all load from the system under test entirely
options.B: Results may not extrapolate reliably to production's capacity and setup
options.C: Careless scripting has no effect on which resources receive load during a test
options.D: Careless scripting always makes a test run with fewer virtual users than configured

questions.explanation: Without variety in requested data or paths, load can pile up on one resource instead of spreading out the way real diverse traffic naturally would.

questions.question: Why is it important to clean up or reset test data between performance test runs?

options.A: Cleaning data removes the need to monitor the system during execution
options.B: Cleaning data guarantees that response times will always improve on the next run
options.C: Cleaning data always increases the total duration of a performance test
options.D: Leftover data from a previous run could skew results or cause functional errors in a later run

questions.explanation: Accumulated or stale data from earlier runs can change database size, cache state or uniqueness constraints in ways that distort later results.

questions.question: Why might a team model "abandonment," where simulated users give up if a page takes too long?

options.A: It removes the need to measure response time in the test
options.B: It is required to make the test script compile in most testing tools
options.C: It guarantees that the system will never experience any errors
options.D: They understand production and help ensure realistic test conditions

questions.explanation: Real users often leave rather than wait indefinitely, so modeling abandonment prevents a workload that unrealistically holds every virtual user in place regardless of delay.

questions.question: Why is documenting the test data used in a performance test important?

options.A: It guarantees that no further performance testing will ever be needed
options.B: It replaces the need to document the test environment configuration
options.C: Moving performance-related activities earlier in the lifecycle
options.D: It is only relevant for functional testing, not performance testing

questions.explanation: Test data characteristics, such as volume and distribution, affect results just as environment configuration does, so both should be documented for reproducibility.

questions.question: Why might a team choose to test pagination behavior specifically as part of performance testing?

options.A: It helps the team learn from data and improve future practices
options.B: Pagination testing is only relevant to the visual design of a page
options.C: Pagination has no effect on database queries or response time
options.D: Pagination testing removes the need to test any other feature

questions.explanation: Inefficient pagination, such as loading entire result sets before slicing them, can become a real performance liability as the underlying data grows.

questions.question: Why should the resource usage of the load-testing tool itself be analyzed during a test?

options.A: Load-testing tools never consume any meaningful CPU or memory themselves
options.B: Analyzing the tool's resource usage removes the need to monitor the system under test
options.C: The tool's resource usage has no bearing on the accuracy of the results it produces
options.D: If the tool or its host machine is overloaded, it may distort or invalidate the results

questions.explanation: A load generator that is itself resource-starved may fail to generate the intended load accurately, which would make the resulting measurements unreliable.

questions.question: Why might a team need more than one performance testing tool on a single project?

options.A: Using more than one tool is always forbidden by every vendor's license agreement
options.B: A single tool is always technically capable of testing any protocol in existence
options.C: Natural variability, so repeats show whether results are consistent
options.D: Using multiple tools removes the need to define a workload model at all

questions.explanation: Systems often combine different technologies, and no single tool necessarily covers every protocol or interface well, so a mix of tools may be needed to test the whole system realistically.

questions.question: Why can a protocol-level (HTTP) load test fail to fully capture client-side performance experienced by real users?

options.A: Protocol-level tests are incapable of sending any HTTP requests at all
options.B: Protocol-level tests can only be used for testing mobile applications
options.C: Investigate whether the test or data was actually representative
options.D: Protocol-level tests always run slower than any browser-based test

questions.explanation: HTTP-level tests measure server-side timing and network round trips but skip what happens once a browser receives the response, such as rendering, which affects the perceived user experience.

questions.question: Why is validating a performance tool's own reported metrics against an independent source sometimes recommended?

options.A: To guarantee that the system under test has zero performance defects
options.B: To remove the need for any monitoring tools during the test
options.C: It lets the results be correctly interpreted and reproduced later
options.D: To make the performance test take significantly longer to complete

questions.explanation: Cross-checking a tool's numbers against another source, such as server-side logs, helps confirm the reported metrics reflect reality rather than an artifact of the tool itself.

questions.question: Why are cloud-based, elastic, pay-per-use load-testing services often attractive for large-scale tests?

options.A: They are always less accurate than infrastructure owned and operated in-house
options.B: Running the planned tests and watching for problems with the run
options.C: They are required by law for any performance test above a certain size
options.D: They eliminate the need to design any workload model for the test

questions.explanation: Elastic, on-demand capacity avoids the cost and effort of maintaining large permanent load-generation infrastructure that would otherwise sit idle between tests.

questions.domain: The Basic Concepts of Performance Testing
questions.question: What is the difference between a "peak" load and an "average" load in an operational profile?

options.A: Peak load is always lower than average load in every operational profile
options.B: Peak load and average load are two names for exactly the same measurement
options.C: Note the error, judge its impact, and decide to stop or restart
options.D: Average load only applies to systems that have no concurrent users at all

questions.explanation: Peak and average describe different points in usage variation: peak captures the busiest moments a system must survive, while average describes typical, everyday conditions.

questions.question: What does a low error rate combined with a high response time most likely suggest about a system under load?

options.A: The monitoring tool has stopped collecting data during the test
options.B: The system is completing requests correctly but slowly, rather than failing outright
options.C: The workload model used in the test was configured with zero virtual users
options.D: The system has already crashed and stopped responding to any requests

questions.explanation: Requests still succeed, so functionality is not the problem; the delay itself is the issue, pointing toward a performance bottleneck rather than a failure.

questions.domain: Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle
questions.question: Why might a team choose to run a smaller performance test earlier against a partially built feature, rather than waiting for the complete feature?

options.A: Early testing gives an initial risk signal while there is still time to influence the design
options.B: Testing a partial feature always produces identical results to testing the complete one
options.C: Early testing removes the need for any further performance testing later on
options.D: Partial features can only be tested for functional correctness, never for performance

questions.explanation: An early, partial signal is more useful than none at all, especially while design choices are still relatively cheap to change.

questions.question: Why might a performance test include deliberately invalid or malformed requests alongside valid ones?

options.A: Testing with invalid requests always produces less realistic results than valid ones alone
options.B: Invalid requests are required to make the load-testing tool function at all
options.C: Malformed requests remove the need to test any of the valid request paths
options.D: To check that error handling does not become a hidden source of excessive load or slow responses

questions.explanation: Error-handling code paths can sometimes be slower or more resource-intensive than the happy path, so including some invalid input gives a more complete performance picture.

questions.question: Why might a team prefer a performance testing tool with strong scripting language support over one with only a visual, no-code interface?

options.A: A no-code interface guarantees more accurate results than any scripted approach
options.B: Visual, no-code tools are incapable of generating any load whatsoever
options.C: Support for scripting and generating the specific network protocols used
options.D: Scripting language support always makes a tool completely free to license

questions.explanation: Real-world workloads sometimes need conditional logic or custom handling that a code-based scripting interface expresses more flexibly than a purely visual builder.
